[F002] The only consumer of `authorizes()` is the F002 write gate at `canonical_backfill.py:334`, which is exactly the path the finding targeted — now backed by genuine OS-level verification.

## Summary

**Finding [high, correctness] — F002 accepts a forged held-lock token:** The auditor showed that `HeldLedgerLock(target=..., _guard=il._LOCK_GUARD).authorizes(...)` returned `True` without any real flock being held, because the only barrier was a process-readable sentinel (`_LOCK_GUARD`) and `authorizes()` decided purely from in-process fields. In Python a module attribute can't be a real privacy/security boundary, so the guard was bypassable.

I moved the security boundary off the forgeable sentinel and onto the **actual OS lock state**. I added `_sidecar_lock_held(target)` in `invocation_ledger.py`, which opens a fresh descriptor to the `<ledger>.lock` sidecar and attempts a non-blocking exclusive `flock`: an `EWOULDBLOCK` means a genuine holder exists (authorized), while a successful acquire means nobody holds it (it releases immediately and returns `False`). Because `flock` locks are bound to the open file description, a separate probe descriptor contends even within the same process when the live `hold_ledger_lock()` context genuinely holds the lock — so the probe truthfully distinguishes held from unheld. `HeldLedgerLock.authorizes()` now requires three gates: `active`, target-path match, and `_sidecar_lock_held(self.target)`. The `_guard` construction check is retained only
